scenes.title: Foundation: inner products and norms

ask.q: When are two real vectors orthogonal?
ask.nudge: Their inner product must be zero.

body: The Euclidean inner product is u·v=Σuᵢvᵢ. The norm is ‖u‖=√(u·u), and two vectors are orthogonal when their inner product is zero.
An orthonormal set is both orthogonal and made of unit vectors. Gram–Schmidt converts an independent set into an orthonormal basis for the same span.

items.ask: What is the projection of v onto a non-zero vector u?
refresh: The projection is the component of v in the direction of u. Subtracting it from v leaves a vector orthogonal to u.
If u is already a unit vector, the denominator u·u is one. The projection becomes (v·u)u.

items.recall: Vectors are pairwise orthogonal and each has norm one.
refresh: Orthogonality means pairwise dot products are zero. Normalisation means every vector has unit length.
An orthonormal basis makes coordinates especially simple: the coordinate of v along basis vector qᵢ is v·qᵢ.

items.recall: A square matrix Q satisfying QᵀQ=I.
refresh: Its columns form an orthonormal basis. Since QᵀQ=I, its inverse is Qᵀ, which makes calculations and coordinate changes efficient.
Orthogonal matrices preserve inner products and lengths: ‖Qx‖=‖x‖. Their determinant is either +1 or −1.

scenes.title: Orthogonal directions separate components

ask.nudge: The coordinates are obtained by simple dot products.

body: Orthogonal directions do not overlap in their inner-product contribution. Projecting onto each basis vector isolates one component.
Normalising the directions makes the coordinate formulas even simpler. This is why orthonormal bases appear in least squares, spectral decomposition and numerical linear algebra.

blocks.body: v=projᵤ(v)+[v−projᵤ(v)], and the residual is orthogonal to u.
For an orthonormal basis q₁,…,qₖ, the projection is Σ(v·qᵢ)qᵢ. The residual is orthogonal to the whole subspace.

scenario.teaser: A vector is decomposed into fitted and residual components.
scenario.title: Projection as the geometry of least squares
body: Least squares projects an observed vector onto the column space of a design matrix. The fitted component lies in the model space, and the residual is orthogonal to that space.
For a one-dimensional subspace spanned by u, the projection formula is ((v·u)/(u·u))u. The residual is the part that cannot be explained along u.
With an orthonormal basis, the projection is a sum of simple dot-product components. This is the geometric reason orthonormal bases are useful in regression and numerical computation.

scenes.title: Gram–Schmidt orthogonalisation
scenes.objective: State the algorithm for an independent set.

ask.q: What do you subtract from v₂ to make it orthogonal to v₁?

blocks.body: uₖ=vₖ−Σⱼ₌₁ᵏ⁻¹projᵤⱼ(vₖ), where u₁,…,uₖ₋₁ are mutually orthogonal.
After obtaining non-zero orthogonal vectors uᵢ, set qᵢ=uᵢ/‖uᵢ‖. The qᵢ form an orthonormal basis for the original span.

scenes.title: Guided: Gram–Schmidt in R²
hints: Subtract to obtain u₂=(1/2,−1/2), then normalise.

solution.say: u₁=(1,1), u₂=(1,0)−(1/2)(1,1)=(1/2,−1/2). Both norms are 1 and 1/√2 respectively, giving q₁=(1,1)/√2 and q₂=(1,−1)/√2.

ask.q: What is the inverse of an orthogonal matrix Q?

blocks.body: Q is orthogonal iff QᵀQ=QQᵀ=I. Hence Q⁻¹=Qᵀ.
‖Qx‖=‖x‖ and (Qx)·(Qy)=x·y. Orthogonal transformations preserve lengths, angles and inner products.
det(Q)²=1, so det(Q)=±1. A real orthogonal matrix represents a rotation or reflection, or a combination.

solution.say: The columns are unit vectors and mutually orthogonal. Therefore QᵀQ=I and Q is orthogonal.

scenes.title: Gram–Schmidt preserves the span
scenes.objective: Understand why orthogonalisation does not change the subspace.

ask.q: Why does replacing v₂ by v₂−projᵤ₁(v₂) preserve the span?
ask.nudge: The new vector is a linear combination of the old vectors.

body: Each Gram–Schmidt vector is obtained by subtracting combinations of earlier vectors. Therefore the new vectors span the same space as the original independent set.
The procedure changes the basis, not the subspace. Normalisation also preserves span because it only multiplies a non-zero vector by a non-zero scalar.

scenario.teaser: A numerical algorithm improves stability by using orthogonal directions.
scenario.title: Orthogonal bases in numerical computation
body: A set of nearly dependent vectors can be difficult to use directly in numerical calculations. Orthogonalisation produces directions with zero pairwise inner products, reducing interference between components.

Gram–Schmidt preserves the span while replacing the original generators by orthogonal vectors. Normalising them gives an orthonormal basis that is convenient for projections and coordinate calculations.
In numerical practice, modified Gram–Schmidt or QR methods may be preferred for better numerical stability, but the classical process is the conceptual foundation.
